extracted.intended_audience: employers, employer legal counsel, and stakeholders subject to or advising on the FTC non-compete final rule
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for employers (and their counsel) to comply with the FTC's final rule banning most non-competes, including notice requirements, exceptions (sale-of-business, accrued causes of action, good-faith), and constitutional/administrative-law reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice timing requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide notice no later than the effective date (i.e., no later than 120 days after the final rule is published in the Federal Register).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rule requires notice by the effective date rather than 45 days after; designed to simplify rule and secure benefits sooner. The Commission finds 120 days is more than adequate and declines to extend the time. This timing applies to workers other than senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice content / safe-harbor model language
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule provides safe harbor model language; the final model uses the phrase '[EMPLOYER NAME] will not enforce any non-compete clause against you.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model language was shortened/clarified from the NPRM. Because this language does not identify the recipient as having a non-compete, employers need not determine which workers have non-competes and may send mass communications. Employers may copy-and-paste the safe harbor model notice to satisfy the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible methods of providing notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may provide notice on paper (hand-delivered or mailed), by email (including current work email or last known personal email), or by text message to a mobile telephone number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 910.2(b)(2) allows text, email, paper by hand or mail to worker's last known street address. Digital formats and mass communications are permitted. Text messages are permissible because they are widely used, fast, low-cost, and effective for workers without email.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of last known contact information / work email
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice may be sent to a worker's last known contact information, including the worker's current work email address or last known personal email address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows employers to use available contact information to provide prompt notice; intended to make compliance practicable and low-burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption when no contact information on file
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer is exempt from the notice requirement for a particular worker if the employer has no record of a street address, email address, mobile telephone number, or other method of contacting the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: § 910.2(b)(3) provides a categorical exemption in rare cases where no contact info exists. This replaces the proposed 'readily available' standard to reduce ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice to former workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide notice to former workers when the employer has contact information for them (same permissible methods as for current workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission deems notice to former workers critical because they may refrain from competitive activity believing they are bound by non-competes. The rule expects most employers to have such contact information and exempts employers only when no contact info exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multilingual notices (optional but encouraged)
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing notices in other languages is optional under § 910.2(b)(6), but employers are encouraged to do so when workers speak languages other than English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid imposing translation burdens, the rule makes translation optional but links to translations of commonly spoken languages (Spanish, Chinese, Arabic, Vietnamese, Tagalog, Korean) to facilitate compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: No individualized-determination burden on employers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because model language does not identify recipients as having a non-compete, employers are not required to determine which workers have non-competes before sending notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permits efficient compliance (e.g., mass emails) and reduces burdens on employers, supporting prompt, wide dissemination of notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on enforcement and representations (scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under § 910.2(a), existing non-competes for workers who are not senior executives are no longer enforceable; the rule also prohibits representing to such workers that they are subject to an enforceable non-compete after the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not rescind agreements retroactively but makes it an unfair method of competition to enforce or represent enforceability beginning on the effective date for workers other than senior executives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for senior executives
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not apply to non-competes entered into with senior executives prior to the effective date; existing agreements with senior executives may continue to be enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission declined to apply the prohibition to senior executives as part of balancing retroactivity/secondary retroactivity concerns and competitive effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale-of-business exception (§ 910.3(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-competes entered into pursuant to a bona fide sale of a business are excepted from the rule; the final rule does not require any ownership-percentage threshold for the seller.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission initially proposed a 25% threshold but removed it in response to comments. The exception is adopted because non-competes ancillary to business sales implicate unique interests; non-competes under this exception remain subject to State law and federal antitrust law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona fide sale standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An excepted non-compete must be entered into pursuant to a bona fide sale — generally a sale made in good faith between two independent parties at arm's length where the seller has a reasonable opportunity to negotiate terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: So-called 'springing' non-competes, repurchase rights, mandatory stock redemptions, sham transactions with wholly owned subsidiaries, and similar schemes are not bona fide sales. Commission declined to list exhaustively which transactions are not bona fide to avoid implying others are allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on evasion schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Transactions or arrangements intended to evade the rule (e.g., sham transactions, springing non-competes, stock-transfer schemes) will not qualify as bona fide sales and are prohibited from using the sale-of-business exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission added the term 'bona fide' and clarifying language to § 910.3(a) to address commenters' concerns about potential abuse and to ensure the exception cannot be gamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception for existing causes of action (§ 910.3(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule does not apply where a cause of action related to a non-compete accrued prior to the effective date (e.g., an alleged breach that occurred before the effective date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exception responds to retroactivity and takings concerns by preserving pre-effective-date causes of action; it is framed to ensure the rule is prospective with respect to enforcement actions that arose earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith exception for representations and enforcement (§ 910.3(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not an unfair method of competition to enforce or attempt to enforce a non-compete clause, or to make representations about a non-compete clause, where a person has a good-faith basis to believe the rule is inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designed to avoid infringing First Amendment protections (e.g., Noerr-Pennington) and to ensure employers with a reasonable, good-faith basis to believe a non-compete is outside Part 910 may act or speak. The rule otherwise prohibits misrepresentations that workers are subject to enforceable non-competes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactivity legal standard and Commission's application
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule is retroactive only if it takes away or impairs vested rights acquired under existing law or creates new obligations or disabilities with respect to past transactions; the Commission finds the final rule is not impermissibly retroactive because it alters only the future enforceability of agreements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission cites precedent (e.g., National Cable) and explains the rule does not render past conduct illegal or sanctionable; to minimize concern it added § 910.3(b) (accrued causes of action exception) and other exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Takings / Penn Central balancing guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether the rule effects a taking, courts apply Penn Central's three factors: economic impact on claimant, interference with investment-backed expectations, and character of government action; the Commission finds the final rule does not constitute a taking under that test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission supports its conclusion by noting non-competes with non-senior workers are rarely bargained-for, employers retain alternatives (NDAs, trade secret law, non-solicitation agreements), provisions allowing renegotiation where non-competes tied to benefits, and that regulation adjusts economic burdens to promote common good rather than performing a physical appropriation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process / administrative notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice-and-comment rulemaking process (NPRM + comments) and subsequent adjudicative processes provide sufficient due process for persons affected by the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission states issuing NPRM and engaging in notice-and-comment satisfies notice and opportunity to be heard; further process exists in administrative adjudication or court before finding a violation.
